title: Air India Flight 171 Crash Probe Enters Final Stages as Investigators Complete Voice Recorder Transcript and Psychological Autopsy
excerpt: India's AAIB expects to finish investigation activities within six weeks, with a court filing revealing the scope of witness interviews and a father's legal battle for answers.
body:
• India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript and conducted a psychological autopsy as part of the Air India Flight 171 crash investigation.
  • The probe, now in its analysis phase, is expected to be completed within approximately six weeks, with a draft final report to follow.
  • A father's lawsuit forced the AAIB to disclose the investigation's progress, after officials allegedly implied his son, the captain, cut fuel to the engines after takeoff.
  • The AAIB says media speculation attributing blame to the pilots has made some witnesses "restrictive and non-responsive."

Investigation Milestones Revealed in Court Filing

India's aircraft accident investigating body has moved into the final stages of its probe into the Air India Flight 171 crash that killed 260 people in June 2025, according to a court filing made on Tuesday. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau disclosed that it has prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript and conducted a psychological autopsy, though it did not identify whose autopsy was performed or reveal any findings.

The Boeing 787 crashed shortly after takeoff from Ahmedabad on June 12, 2025, while en route to London Gatwick. All 242 people aboard died, along with 19 people on the ground — making it the deadliest aviation disaster in Indian history.

The AAIB said investigators had interviewed Air India 787 pilots, crew members who had previously flown with the pilots of the crashed aircraft, technical personnel involved in preparing the jet, air traffic controllers, weather officials, and human-factors specialists, according to Reuters.

A Father's Legal Fight for Answers

The details emerged only because of a lawsuit filed by Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, the father of the flight's captain. Sabharwal said AAIB officials who visited his residence during the early stages of the investigation implied that his son had cut the fuel to the plane's engines after takeoff — an allegation that devastated the family and prompted the legal action.

"Media speculation and narratives attributing blame to the pilots had caused some witnesses to become restrictive and non-responsive."

— Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau, court filing

The lawsuit compelled the AAIB to make disclosures about the investigation's scope and timeline that it had not previously shared publicly. In its filing, the bureau acknowledged that speculation in the media had complicated its work, noting that some witnesses had become uncooperative.

Engine Data and Organizational Factors Still Pending

While the voice recorder transcript and psychological autopsy are complete, critical work remains. The AAIB said an analysis of data retrieved in late May from an engine monitoring unit was still awaited, and an assessment of certain organizational factors was still in progress, without providing further details.

The bureau said the probe was now in its analysis phase, with findings and conclusions being drawn across operational, technical, human-factors, and organizational areas. It expects remaining investigation activities to be completed within approximately six weeks, subject to pending "external dependencies."

Separately, the bureau opposed requests from victims' families for access to the cockpit voice recordings, citing Rule 17(5) of India's Aircraft (Investigation of Accidents and Incidents) Rules, 2025, which imposes an absolute prohibition on public disclosure of cockpit audio. "This is an absolute statutory prohibition," the AAIB stated in its filing, according to Bar and Bench.

Questions That Remain

The crash has drawn intense scrutiny because preliminary findings suggested no mechanical or maintenance issues with the aircraft. Air India CEO Campbell Wilson had said in an internal memo that the preliminary report found no mechanical failure, and the AAIB issued no safety recommendations for Boeing or engine manufacturer GE — focusing attention squarely on human factors in the cockpit.

Earlier reports indicated that fuel cutoff switches in the cockpit were moved to the off position seconds after takeoff, a finding described as "very disturbing" by Peter Goelz, a former managing director of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board.

The investigation's completion will be closely watched by the global aviation industry and by the families of the victims, many of whom were members of the Indian diaspora traveling between India and the UK. The crash prompted renewed debate over cockpit video recorders and pilot mental health screening across international aviation.

What Comes Next

If the AAIB meets its six-week timeline, investigation activities would wrap up by late August, with a draft final report to follow. The probe is structured as an internationally coordinated investigation involving the State of Registry, State of Operator, State of Design, and State of Manufacture through accredited representatives, which the AAIB cited as a factor in the investigation's duration.

For the families still seeking answers more than a year after the tragedy, the filing represents the most detailed public accounting of the investigation's progress to date — even as the AAIB maintains its position that the probe's purpose is to improve aviation safety, not to assign blame.
